title: 3-Read Friday #25: Questioning Technique, Messy Markbooks, and GCSE Revision
author: Craig Barton
summary: Issue 25 leads with Adam Boxer's "Step away from the speaker," which Barton frames as characteristic of Boxer's skill at turning evidence into concrete classroom moves, admitting he's repeated the very unexamined habit - stepping toward a student who's answering - that Boxer's post identifies and corrects. His second pick, David Didau's piece on messy markbooks and clipboard tracking, gets filtered through Barton's own maths-teaching context: mini-whiteboards solve the problem of seeing every student's answer at once, but Cold Call remains necessary for open-ended responses, and Didau's tracking system addresses the separate challenge of remembering who still needs to be checked on. Barton closes, as he often does, with a lighter resource-focused pick - Jo Morgan's GCSE Revision list, praised as coming from the official Queen of Resources - explicitly framed as a treat for the maths geeks rather than substantive argument. Two of the issue's three selections concern the specific mechanics of classroom questioning: what a teacher does physically when a student answers, and how a teacher tracks who's been asked what across a lesson.
points: Barton's framing of Adam Boxer's piece is personally implicating - he admits to having repeated the exact unexamined habit that Boxer's post interrogates.

He connects David Didau's messy-markbook technique to his own maths-specific practice, noting mini-whiteboards solve the seeing-every-answer problem but not the separate problem of tracking who's been Cold Called.

Barton's closing pick, Jo Morgan's GCSE Revision resource list, is explicitly bracketed as a lighter, resource-focused finish rather than an argument piece, continuing a pattern of ending issues on curated resources.
Two of three picks this issue concern classroom questioning mechanics specifically - what happens physically and organizationally around asking and tracking student answers.
quotes: Adam is one of the finest translators of evidence into concrete classroom strategies, and this post is a great example of that.
Adam examines a practice I have done 1000s of times without giving it a single thought - what I do when a child is giving an answer - highlights the issue, and then suggests how we can improve it.
In maths, it is pretty easy to see the answers of all students at the same time to most questions using a mini-whiteboard. But that doesn't mean Cold Call should be abandoned altogether.
But keeping track of who I have Cold Called and, more importantly, who I need to question again or speak to later in the lesson, can be tricky.
The official Queen of Resources, Jo Morgan, has compiled a super useful list of all the best places to find either topic-specific or mixed-topic revision materials.
